steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Verse literature exams test translation, analysis of poetic features, and evaluation of themes and characterisation — always with reference to the Latin text.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: When analysing style, always PEA: Point (name the feature), Evidence (quote the Latin), Analysis (explain the effect on the reader).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Common poetic features to discuss: alliteration, enjambement, elision, caesura, onomatopoeia, hyperbaton, simile, metaphor, and word order.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: For evaluation questions on character or theme, structure your answer with an introduction, 3-4 paragraphs each with a Latin quotation, and a conclusion.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What does PEA stand for and why is it important? | Q: List six poetic features you should be prepared to discuss. | Q: How should you structure a 10-mark evaluation question?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Point, Evidence, Analysis. Make a point about a feature, quote the Latin as evidence, and analyse the effect. This ensures every analytical claim is supported by textual evidence. | Alliteration, enjambement, elision, caesura, onomatopoeia, hyperbaton, simile, metaphor, word order, assonance (any six). | Introduction stating your thesis, 3-4 paragraphs each with PEA (point supported by Latin quotation and analysis), and a brief conclusion.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Prepare a 'style toolkit' for each author before the exam: know their characteristic devices and effects. In the exam, read the question twice and underline key words. For translation, work through the Latin methodically: identify the verb, then subjects and objects, then subordinate clauses. Never write a paragraph without a Latin quotation in it.
